summary: Establishes an IANA registry of FTP command and feature names, to reduce name conflicts as extensions to FTP keep growing. It builds on the extension negotiation mechanism of RFC 2389 and the commands summarized in RFC 959. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It is a shared phone book of command names for a file-sending tool, so no two people give the same name to different commands.

subtitle: An IANA registry that keeps FTP command names and extension names from colliding.

tldr.problem: FTP keeps gaining new commands and extensions, and not all of them are announced through the FEAT mechanism, so names could clash and cause ambiguity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates an IANA registry called "FTP Commands and Extensions", defines what each entry records, sets Expert Review as the registration method, and fills in the initial contents with the base, historic and extension commands.
tldr.outcome: FTP implementers get one place to look up command and feature names. It updates RFC 959 and introduces no new security issues.

sections.title: Why FTP Needs a Registry
sections.content:
Every version of the FTP specification has added a few new commands, and the early ones are summarized in RFC 959. RFC 2389 then set up a way to negotiate extensions: a server lists the extensions it supports as FEAT strings in reply to a FEAT command.

The number of extensions keeps growing, and not all of them use FEAT. To reduce the chance of two extensions using the same name, and the confusion that follows, this RFC establishes an IANA registry and encourages sharing of information about extensions.
sections.eli5: People keep inventing new commands for a file-sending tool. Without a list, two people might pick the same name for different things. The list stops that.

sections.title: What a Registry Entry Records
sections.content:
The registry is named "FTP Commands and Extensions". Each registration request and entry should include the following fields.

  • Command Name: the FTP command, in all uppercase. A plus sign (+) is appended when an extension amends how a command works. If an extension affects overall parameter handling or transactions, the string -N/A- is used. Entries are ordered by ascending ASCII collation of this column.
  • Extension name: shown in a column titled "FEAT Code".
  • Description: a brief description.
  • FEAT String: optional, only needed when the string in a FEAT response has mandatory elements beyond the FEAT code. IANA shows these in numbered footnotes.
  • Command Type: a (access control), p (transfer parameter) or s (service), following Section 4.1 of RFC 959. Combinations such as p/s are allowed.
  • Conformance: m for mandatory, o for optional, h for historic.
  • Reference: an RFC or other definition.
sections.eli5: Each line in the list says the command's name, what it does, which kind it is, whether you must support it, and where to read about it.

sections.title: FEAT Codes and Placeholders
sections.content:
Older FTP extensions, and some newer ones, never defined a keyword for FEAT responses. So the RFC creates placeholder keywords (also called pseudo FEAT codes) to reserve reasonable names for future standardization. The basic RFC 959 commands also get placeholders. These are not meant to be returned in FEAT responses.

True FEAT codes are listed in uppercase and placeholders in lowercase. A future specification may upgrade a placeholder to a real keyword unless it is declared immutable. IANA keeps FEAT codes unique using a case-insensitive comparison.
sections.eli5: Some commands had no nickname, so the list gives them a temporary one written in small letters. Real nicknames are written in capitals.

sections.title: Who Can Register
sections.content:
The registry is meant to avoid conflicting names, not to show that an extension is somehow approved. Registration uses Expert Review, but the designated expert only checks that at least one of two criteria is met: the extension is documented in a permanent, readily available public specification, or it is actually implemented in generally available FTP clients and servers.

Marking an entry mandatory (m) requires an IETF Standards Track specification. Beyond the initial registrations, Standards Action is needed to register new mandatory entries or to move them to historic. An IESG Standards Action may also direct IANA to change the conformance of any entry.
sections.eli5: To get on the list, you only need a public write-up or a tool people can really get. Nobody has to say your idea is good.

sections.title: Base and Obsolete Commands
sections.content:
The commands from RFC 959 are listed with the immutable placeholder base. The mandatory ones are ABOR, ACCT, ALLO, APPE, CWD, DELE, HELP, LIST, MODE, NLST, NOOP, PASS, PASV, PORT, QUIT, REIN, REST, RETR, RNFR, RNTO, SITE, STAT, STOR, STRU, TYPE and USER. The optional ones are CDUP, MKD, PWD, RMD, SMNT, STOU and SYST. STD 3 (RFC 1123) clarified several of these.

Two groups are marked historic, with the immutable placeholder hist. XCUP, XCWD, XMKD, XPWD and XRMD came from an early experimental extension (RFC 775) and were deprecated by RFC 1123 because standard FTP has successors. The RFC notes that deployed clients still use them and most servers support them as aliases. LPRT and LPSV came from the "FOOBAR" effort in RFC 1545 and RFC 1639 and are now obsolete.
sections.eli5: The list keeps the old, retired commands too, because some programs still use them and nobody should reuse their names.

sections.title: Initial Contents
sections.content:
The registry started with all FTP commands and features published in RFCs after STD 3 up to the time of writing. Besides base and hist, three more placeholders were assigned: secu for FTP Security Extensions (RFC 2228), feat for Feature Negotiation (RFC 2389) and nat6 for FTP Extensions for NAT/IPv6 (RFC 2428).

Table 1 lists each command, such as MDTM, MLST, MLSD and SIZE from RFC 3659, and AUTH and PBSZ from the security extensions. Footnotes give FEAT strings, for example AUTH TLS for RFC 4217 and REST STREAM for the restart extension.
sections.eli5: The first version of the list was filled in by collecting every command that had already been written down.

sections.title: IANA and Security Notes
sections.content:
IANA established the registry using the content in Section 3 and the text of Sections 2.4 and 2.5 as a preface. New entries should be added when extensions are approved or defined in RFCs, or when extensions already in use and well-documented are identified.

The security section is short: the registry provides improved documentation and protection against interoperability problems, and it introduces no new security issues.
sections.eli5: A list of names cannot hurt anyone. It just helps everybody understand each other.
